knowledge.text: Under the current joint edit, which extended the anti-repetition/coverage search discipline from multi-instance to all unmet tasks (including single-object clean/put tasks) and added a stop-searching-once-the-exact-target-is-held clause, candidate post-acquisition sequences remained productive and identical to the parent for put some mug on sidetable (P3/Q3, 4 steps), put some pencil on desk (P5/Q5, 5), clean butterknife in drawer (P6/Q6, 8), and clean soapbar in toilet (P9/Q9, 7). Candidate was much faster in put a mug in sidetable (Q4 4 steps vs P4 12): Q4 went directly to diningtable1, took mug1, and placed it on sidetable1, while P4 opened drawer1 and drawer2 and visited drawer3, drawer4, sidetable1, and sidetable2 before taking mug1 from diningtable1; this is consistent with a search-order shortcut but is not isolated from stochastic location choice. However, the candidate still cycled even when the target was reachable in cool some apple and put it in microwave, revisiting fridge1, countertop1, cabinet1, and countertop2 before reaching diningtable1 at Q10:13 and taking 19 steps versus P10's 15, though both succeeded and preserved the cool-then-place sequence.

In single-object clean-and-place tasks where the target was not found, both sides reached the 50-step limit with repeated revisiting, so the extended anti-revisit/coverage guidance did not ensure coverage of plausible locations or stop long recheck loops. In clean some butterknife and put it in drawer, P7 and Q7 both cycled among drawer1, drawer2, drawer3, countertop1, countertop2, and cabinets, and neither acquired a butterknife. In put a clean soapbar in cabinet, P8 and Q8 both cycled among cabinet1-4, countertop1, sinkbasin1, and bathtubbasin1, and neither acquired a soapbar. These are step-limit terminations; they do not establish target absence, only that the guidance did not produce a successful acquisition in these runs.

The added stop-searching-once-the-exact-target-is-held clause was not reliably followed in a single-object desklamp task. In examine the bowl with the desklamp, Q1 held bowl1 from Q1:2 but then examined bowl1 (Q1:3) and went to shelf1 (Q1:4) before returning to desk1 and finally using desklamp1 at dresser1, succeeding in 7 steps; P1 reached the same success in 4 steps. Thus the candidate did not stop searching upon holding the target and was less efficient here, though the single case and stochastic choices limit causal attribution to this clause.

The new Exact Object Type clause was followed in the one applicable case but without task-completion benefit. In clean some butterknife and put it in drawer, parent P7 saw knife1 and spatula1 in the opened drawer1 and took the wrong-type knife1 (P7:5), cleaned it (P7:7), and moved it to drawer1 (P7:9), then continued searching and hit the step limit; candidate Q7 saw the same knife1 in open drawer1 at Q7:4 but did not take it, never acquired any object, and also hit the step limit, with no butterknife found by either side. Thus the clause was associated with avoiding the wrong-type acquisition (a knife where a butterknife was required) but did not yield the required object or task success, and no case tested the do-not-repeat-a-wrong-type-placement provision. In the tasks where both sides used the correct type (clean butterknife in drawer P6/Q6, clean soapbar in toilet P9/Q9), the procedures remained identical successes.
